summary: Specifies how to use the Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP) as the application transport for the Internet Registry Information Service (IRIS).

eli5.summary: IRIS needs a vehicle to carry its questions and answers. This memo picks one called BEEP and explains how to load it.

questions: what is the iris.beep uri scheme
subtitle: How registry lookups from IRIS ride on top of BEEP sessions over TCP, with TLS-based server checks.

tldr.problem: IRIS, the Internet Registry Information Service, needs an application transport that provides framing, authentication and negotiation, without inventing a new one.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC maps IRIS onto BEEP: a BEEP profile URI names the IRIS version and registry type, each request is an MSG answered by an RPY, and TLS is used to check the server's identity over TCP.
tldr.outcome: It defines the iris.beep URI scheme and registrations, plus a checklist of what each registry type must say about message patterns and server authentication. It is a Proposed Standard, and RFC 8996 updates it.

facts.label: Default pattern
facts.value: One MSG, one RPY, ERR for faults

today: RFC 3983 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8996. It has not been obsoleted according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why BEEP Carries IRIS
sections.content:
RFC 3983 describes the application transport binding that lets IRIS (the Internet Registry Information Service, defined in RFC 3981) run over BEEP (the Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol, RFC 3080). The requirements come from the CRISP requirements in RFC 3707.

The RFC gives three reasons for choosing BEEP. It is an existing, well-understood protocol with the needed features, so implementers get toolkits and debugging gear and operators can reuse deployment experience. A purpose-built transport would end up similar but probably smaller and less complete once framing and authentication are counted.

It also explains why not the alternatives. HTTP is rejected because IRIS is not meant to bypass firewalls or to be confused with ordinary web applications, and because of the guidelines in RFC 3205 and the muddle over how TLS is used with HTTP. Plain TCP, as in the EPP-TCP draft, lacks the client negotiation that IRIS needs when one client follows referrals across several servers with different parameters.
sections.eli5: Instead of building a brand new delivery truck, the authors borrowed a proven one that already has good locks and labels. Other trucks were either too easy to confuse with web traffic or too plain.

sections.title: The BEEP Profile Identifier
sections.content:
A BEEP profile names what a channel is used for. For IRIS, the profile identifier is a URI made of the IRIS schema URN, a slash, and an IRIS registry type URN. Both URNs MUST be abbreviated using the rules of IRIS. The ABNF is profile = profile-uri "/" iris-urn-abbrev "/" registry-urn-abbrev, with profile-uri set to http://iana.org/beep/.

The RFC's example is http://iana.org/beep/iris1/dreg1, which selects IRIS version urn:iana:params:xml:ns:iris1 and the registry type urn:iana:params:xml:ns:dreg1.

This URI goes in the profile element when a BEEP channel is created. BEEP lets a client offer several profile elements, so the IRIS version can be negotiated for each registry type a server offers. Once the profile is accepted, the channel is ready for IRIS messages, and a server MUST honor queries for all advertised registry types on any channel opened with an IRIS profile URI.
sections.eli5: The profile name is like a ticket that says which game you want to play and which version of the rules. The client can hand over several tickets, and the server picks one it knows.

sections.title: Message Packages and Encoding
sections.content:
The profile carries XML that holds IRIS requests and responses. These XML instances MUST be encoded as Unicode and use the media type application/xml according to RFC 3023.

On character encodings the RFC is specific. XML processors must recognize UTF-8 and UTF-16. With no encoding attribute and no byte order mark, the default is UTF-8. For compatibility, and per RFC 2277, UTF-8 is RECOMMENDED, UTF-16 is OPTIONAL, and other encodings MUST NOT be used.

A registry type MAY also define message packages that are not IRIS XML, for example binary images referenced by an IRIS response.
sections.eli5: The messages are written in a standard text format, and everybody should use the same alphabet so letters do not get scrambled on the way.

sections.title: Message Patterns
sections.content:
Each registry type is defined by its own BEEP profile, so each MAY define a different message pattern, as long as it stays within what BEEP allows. If a registry type defines none, the default pattern applies. Every registry type MUST be able to support the default pattern for the <lookupEntity> query in IRIS.

The default pattern is a single one-to-one request and response. The client sends an IRIS XML instance in a BEEP MSG message. The server answers with an RPY message that also holds an IRIS XML instance. The ERR message is used for fault codes, and the allowed codes are those listed in BEEP.
sections.eli5: The normal conversation is one question and one answer. If something goes wrong, the server sends a special error note instead of an answer.

sections.title: Server Authentication
sections.content:
When the BEEP TLS tuning profile is used, a client can verify the server, but a convention must say which authority name the client asks credentials for. Because that depends on the authority part of the URI, each registry type SHOULD define a server authentication method. If it does not, the basic server authentication method applies.

The basic method works in four steps:

  • The client MUST present the authority name using the BEEP serverName mechanism. Resolving iris:dreg1//com/domain/example.com means using serverName="com".
  • During TLS negotiation the server presents an X.509 certificate for that authority. It MUST contain the authority in the subjectDN or in a dNSName entry of the subjectAltName extension.
  • The certificate MUST be cryptographically verified under the TLS procedures.
  • The client then checks the subject for a case-insensitive match, in this order: a dNSName in subjectAltName; a subjectDN made only of dc components (example.com is dc=example, dc=com); or a subjectDN whose left-most component is a cn holding the authority name, where an asterisk wildcard MAY be the left-most label.

If no component matches, the certificate is invalid for that authority.
sections.eli5: Before trusting a server, the client asks for its ID card and checks that the name on it matches the place it meant to visit. If the names do not match, the card is rejected.

sections.title: Transport Mapping and Registrations
sections.content:
IRIS requires each transport mapping to define a few items. Here the URI scheme name and the application protocol label are both iris.beep. Allowed character sets are covered by the encoding rules in the message section and the internationalization section. The mapping is specific to RFC 3080 and MUST use TCP as specified by RFC 3081.

The RFC then lists registrations for IANA: the BEEP profile (http://iana.org/beep/iris1, with IRIS XML instances starting exchanges and in positive replies, and no messages in negative replies or one-to-many exchanges), the iris.beep URI scheme, a well-known TCP port entry named "IRIS over BEEP" with no broadcast or multicast, and an S-NAPTR application protocol label.

Finally, specifications of registry types MUST state a message pattern (their own, or the default) and a server authentication method (their own, the basic one, or none at all).
sections.eli5: The memo fills in the official forms that give the new service its name and labels, and gives future registry designers a checklist of what they have to decide.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementers are told to know the security considerations of IRIS, BEEP and TLS, and to see the server authentication rules above. Clients SHOULD be prepared to use several BEEP tuning profiles: SASL DIGEST-MD5 or OTP for user authentication without session encryption, and TLS for encryption, optionally with client-side certificates. The listed TLS cipher suites are TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA, TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA and TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA.

Anonymous client access SHOULD be done either with no authentication tuning profile or with the SASL ANONYMOUS profile.

Because IRIS uses referrals as a normal part of operation, user credentials must not be handed to untrusted servers. So clients SHOULD NOT use SASL PLAIN, and MUST NOT use it unless the TCP session is first encrypted, for example with the TLS tuning profile.
sections.eli5: Since a lookup can send you on to other servers, you should not tell your secret password in the open. Use locked channels, and only show a password where it is safe.
